source.title: Spectra: Surprising Effectiveness of Pretraining Ternary Language Models at Scale
source.authors: Ayush Kaushal; Tejas Pandey; Tejas Vaidhya; Arnab Kumar Mondal; Aaryan Bhagat; Irina Rish

record.tranche_reason: The paper measures validation loss across parameter scales and fits scaling curves, but applies this to ternary and floating-point model families with its own training setup and fitting analysis.
record.gate_note: The study varies model size and measures validation loss at a fixed 300B-token training regime. It does not test compute-optimal parameter/token allocations or predict actual larger-run losses from smaller-run fits. Training-loss curves and downstream benchmark results are distinct from held-out validation-loss scaling; only benchmark aggregates and LAMBADA accuracy are included here for V6. The other reported benchmark tables are not exhaustively extracted.
record.test_reason: The study fits final validation loss against parameter count (99M–3.9B, fixed 300B tokens) for ternary-weight TriLMs and FP16 FloatLMs, compares offset and plain power-law fits, and reports downstream accuracy across scale. Its own results bear on V1, V6 and V7 in a new setting: ternary-weight models.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that TriLMs scale better than FloatLMs in model size (bits), and that offset power-law fits show the TriLM–FloatLM validation-loss gap shrinking with N. At 3.9B, TriLM matches FloatLM downstream despite higher perplexity. The offset fit is described as slightly more precise than a plain power law. Scaling across data regimes is left as future work.
record.recipe_differences: Measures validation loss across model sizes as in scaling-law studies, but uses ternary and floating-point families trained on a fixed 300B-token corpus and compares offset and standard power-law fitting.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports standard power-law fits as slightly less precise than offset fits; results are limited to the stated 300B-token training regime.
record.problems: The parameter sweep is 99M–3.9B and thus does not span several orders of magnitude; only a fixed 300B-token data regime is used for the reported scaling fits. The paper derives very-large-scale comparisons from fitted laws rather than evaluating those larger models. No uncertainty is reported for the scaling-fit parameters.
record.rows_left_out: The individual downstream scores in Tables 6, 9, 10, 11, 12, and 13 are not exhaustively extracted; for V6, Table 7 six-benchmark averages, Table 9 LAMBADA accuracy, and the text's explicit LogiQA trend statement were retained. Figure 13's separate corpus perplexity comparison and the training-loss curves were left out because they do not provide the tested held-out parameter-scaling comparison in V1.

untested.parts: Scaling in tokens or compute; parameter range of several orders of magnitude (only 99M–3.9B tested); data held fixed at 300B tokens rather than non-bottlenecking.
Not tested. The paper extrapolates its fits to 15.6B and 330B parameters but never checks the predictions against actual runs.
Not tested; there is no fixed-compute allocation search.
Not tested; shapes vary with size, with no fixed-N comparison.
Not tested; no other modalities, repeated data, fine-tuning or transfer.
Parameter counting, training schedule and data effects on the exponents are not varied.

missing.what: Cross-family loss-vs-downstream mismatch: TriLM 3.9B has the validation loss of FloatLM 1.1B but downstream scores close to FloatLM 3.9B, despite higher perplexity
TriviaQA non-monotonic for TriLM (830M 4.3 → 1.1B 1.9 exact match); TruthfulQA near random across all scales
BiLM vs TriLM validation-loss scaling across parameters (99M, 560M, 1.1B)

record.verdict_notes: Tranche set to T3 (a new setting, ternary-weight LMs) rather than the reader's T2. The reader's V1 limits_scope label about the narrow parameter range was dropped: that range is an untested part, not a qualifying result. Extrapolations to 15.6B and 330B are predictions, not tests of V2.

versions.untested_parts: Tests validation loss versus parameter count for TriLM and FloatLM at a fixed 300B-token data regime; does not test scaling versus token count or compute, nor several orders of magnitude in parameter count.
No reported comparison of predictions fitted on small runs with actual runs orders of magnitude larger.
No fixed-compute-budget search for the loss-minimising parameter/token split.
No controlled comparison of depth, width, or other architectural choices at fixed parameter count.
No other modalities, repeated-data regimes, fine-tuning, or transfer scaling tests.
Reports zero-shot downstream benchmark performance across model scales, including a six-task average and LAMBADA accuracy; does not test predictability from pretraining loss.
Compares standard power-law and offset power-law fits for the tested families; does not systematically vary parameter counting, training schedule, data, or other fitting choices.

rows.subject: TriLM family (99M–3.9B)
rows.operation_detail: Fit validation loss against parameter count with an offset power law.
rows.measure: Final validation loss; fitted parameters A=185, α=0.26, ϵ=1.76
rows.value: A=185, α=0.26, ϵ=1.76; the text states the fitted law has shared scaling exponent α=0.26 and offset ϵ=1.76
rows.note: Fit is reported for the TriLM family as a whole; the authors describe validation loss as improving consistently with parameter count.
rows.check: State holds for loss falling with N. No goodness-of-fit or fit uncertainty is reported. The sweep spans only about 1.6 orders of magnitude, so the 'several orders' part is untested, not observed.

relationships.condition: TriLM and FloatLM, 99M–3.9B parameters, 300B tokens, offset power-law fit
relationships.reason: Validation loss falls with N and is fitted by a power law with offset, shared α=0.26 (r1, r2). Fit quality is not quantified.
relationships.display_finding: Validation loss decreased with parameters and fit offset power laws with shared exponent α = 0.26.

source_check.label: supports
source_check.condition: TriLM and FloatLM, 99M–3.9B parameters, 300B tokens, offset power-law fit
source_check.reason: §4.3 fits decreasing validation loss with inverse-power-plus-offset laws and α=0.26 for both families (r1,r2). Several orders of magnitude and freedom from data bottlenecks remain untested.

relationships.condition: Offset vs plain power-law fit on the same 300B-token runs
relationships.reason: The exponent changes from 0.26 to about 0.09 depending on whether an offset is fitted. The families' exponents are identical in one form and differ in the other (0.093 vs 0.085) (r1–r4).
relationships.display_finding: The exponent changes from 0.26 to about 0.09 when fitting an offset, with identical family exponents in one formulation versus 0.093 and 0.085 in the other.

source_check.label: supports
source_check.condition: Offset vs plain power-law fit on the same 300B-token runs
source_check.reason: §4.3 and Appendix C report α=0.26 with offsets versus plain-fit exponent magnitudes 0.093 for TriLM and 0.085 for FloatLM (r1–r4); fit uncertainty is unreported.

relationships.condition: FloatLM six-task average and LAMBADA; TriLM from 190M up
relationships.reason: Averages and LAMBADA accuracy rise with each scale step in FloatLM and in most TriLM steps (r7–r13, r15–r22, r24–r28, r30–r31, r33–r40).
relationships.display_finding: Six-task averages and LAMBADA accuracy increase at every FloatLM size step and at most TriLM steps from 190M upward.

source_check.label: supports
source_check.condition: FloatLM six-task average and LAMBADA; TriLM from 190M up
source_check.reason: Tables 7 and 9 show FloatLM averages and LAMBADA accuracy increasing at every size step; TriLM averages increase from 190M onward and LAMBADA generally improves, with the separately identified plateau.

relationships.reason: The TriLM average drops from 99M to 190M (43.5→42.4, r6). TriLM LAMBADA is flat from 1.1B to 1.5B (r29). LogiQA shows no trend near chance across all scales (r41).
relationships.display_finding: TriLM average performance fell from 43.5 at 99M to 42.4 at 190M, LAMBADA was flat from 1.1B to 1.5B, and LogiQA stayed near chance without a scaling trend.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.reason: Table 7 gives TriLM averages 43.5 at 99M and 42.4 at 190M; Table 9 gives LAMBADA accuracy 46.2 at both 1.1B and 1.5B. §5 explicitly reports no clear LogiQA performance trend.

relationships.condition: Predicting downstream performance from validation loss across TriLM vs FloatLM
relationships.reason: Text-based, no row. TriLM 3.9B matches the validation loss of FloatLM 1.1B but scores 60.7 vs 54.9 on the average. It roughly matches FloatLM 3.9B downstream despite higher validation loss. So the loss-to-downstream mapping depends on weight precision.
relationships.display_finding: TriLM 3.9B matched FloatLM 1.1B validation loss but scored 60.7 versus 54.9, and roughly matched FloatLM 3.9B downstream despite higher loss.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.condition: Predicting downstream performance from validation loss across TriLM vs FloatLM
source_check.reason: §4.3 states that TriLM 3.9B matches FloatLM 1.1B validation loss; Table 7 gives their averages as 60.7 and 54.9. TriLM 3.9B approaches FloatLM 3.9B downstream performance despite higher validation loss, qualifying a precision-independent loss-to-performance mapping.
